edges.effect_quant: The alpha-blocker class has a longstanding postural blood-pressure liability, though the magnitude varies by agent. In a randomized antihypertensive trial of two alpha-1 blockers, orthostatic symptoms were significantly more frequent and severe with prazosin than bunazosin. BPH trials and reviews also show that older nonselective agents such as doxazosin lower blood pressure measurably, whereas uroselective tamsulosin produces fewer orthostatic findings.
edges.population: adults prescribed alpha-1 adrenergic antagonists for hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia, or lower urinary tract symptoms
edges.mechanism: Alpha-blockers reduce peripheral vascular tone and blunt reflex vasoconstriction when standing, which can impair blood-pressure maintenance during postural change. Older, less uroselective agents tend to produce more systemic vasodilation and therefore more orthostatic symptoms.
edges.summary: This is a real but heterogeneous harmful class effect. Orthostatic hypotension is part of the alpha-blocker safety profile, especially with older or less selective agents, although modern uroselective drugs like tamsulosin appear to attenuate rather than eliminate that risk.
edges.caveats: The strongest direct orthostatic evidence is older and often agent-specific, so the class estimate should not be interpreted as uniform across every alpha-blocker. The most accurate read is that orthostatic risk is built into the mechanism, but it is substantially modified by receptor selectivity, dose titration, age, and comedications.
